newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels guard hostages with a fearsome arsenal.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels guard hostages with a fearsome arsenal.

text.p: The Marxist rebels holding the Japanese embassy residence in Lima have booby-trapped entrances and guard hostages with a fearsome arsenal of explosives and guns, former hostages and police say.

The guerrillas demonstrated their firepower when they stormed the fortified compound on Dec. 17, blowing a hole in the perimeter wall with explosives before swarming in, guns blazing, to capture 500 mainly VIP guests at a reception.

Respect for their military capacity has grown since then with revelations of meticulous six-month training in Peru's Amazon jungle, thorough preparations inside the residence for a possible attack from outside and a large stock of weapons.
"We're not underestimating them. They are hard, really hard, but not just that. They are smart as well," one source in the anti-terrorism police said.

Austrian Ambassador Arthur Schuschnigg, freed on Sunday along with a big group of other hostages, told reporters each of the roughly 20 rebels had 33 pounds (15 kg) of explosives strapped to his or her belt, with a ring to detonate them.
Other freed captives said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels had mined the entrances to the residence to deter an attack from Peruvian security forces.
Three or four snipers with infrared telescopic night sights stand guard round the clock at strategic windows, police said. Each rebel has an AKM automatic rifle and a commando knife.

Rebels also have the advantage of the embassy residence's wealth of security features designed to deter intruders. These include windows doubly protected by bars and thick meshed wire grilles, plus a high perimeter wall.
They no longer have the benefit of the closed circuit television cameras that monitored the garden outside, however, because all electric power has been cut.

"If we go in, there's going to be a hellish battle, I can guarantee you that," said Jonny Rojas, a special operations policeman patrolling a street outside the residence. "Personally, I think it's worth the cost, but the politicians wouldn't agree."
The Peruvian government stationed 900 police officers around the residence and has crack troops on hand to storm the building as a last resort.

Besides the military capacity of the rebels, security forces have to contend with another MRTA unit apparently hiding elsewhere in Lima and ready to strike other targets in case of an assault on their comrades.
President Alberto Fujimori only spoke publicly once since the crisis began, urging the rebels to lay down their arms and free all the hostages before a "way out" could be considered.
He spent most of his time in war Cabinets with a small inner circle of top generals, senior intelligence officers, ministers and close advisers.

Anti-terrorism police sources believe a strike on the residence would need at least 10 commandos for each rebel. It would last between three and five minutes and could result in the death or injury of up to 20 percent of the 104 captives, according to calculations based on past experience.
Police sources said they had a healthy respect for the muscular, well-trained rebels, who are mainly between 16 and 20 years old and include two women.
The MRTA fighters came to Lima for the operation from the "Atahualpa Front" in Chanchamayo province, 220 miles (350 km) east of Lima in the Amazon jungle.

According to one newspaper report on Thursday, the movement spent up to $300,000 on preparations for the assault, training, arms purchases and a $5,000 payment to each of the fighters involved in the assault.
Apart from the initial battle during the storming of the residence, there have been only two explosions and two gunshots, all unexplained, at the residence.
